questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}-\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function satisfying $f\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=\frac{f(x)}{f(y)}$ for all $x,y,f(y)\neq0$. If $f'(1)=2024$, then :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the functional equation in $x$ only, then put $y=x$ so that $f'(1)$ appears.
solution: Differentiate partially with respect to $x$, keeping $y$ fixed: $f'\left(\frac xy\right)\cdot\frac1y=\frac{f'(x)}{f(y)}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Turn the equation into $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ and differentiate in $y$ at $y=1$.
solution: Replace $y$ by $\frac1y$ in the given relation: $f(xy)=\frac{f(x)}{f(1/y)}=f(x)f(y)$, so $f$ is multiplicative.

useful_results: $f\left(\frac xy\right)=\frac{f(x)}{f(y)}$ gives $f(1)=1$, $f\left(\frac1y\right)=\frac1{f(y)}$ and $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$; a differentiable multiplicative function is $x^k$ (for $x>0$) with $k=f'(1)$, so $xf'(x)=kf(x)$.
Companion forms: $f(x+y)=f(x)f(y)\Rightarrow f=e^{kx}$ with $f'(x)=f'(0)f(x)$; $f(xy)=f(x)+f(y)\Rightarrow f=k\ln|x|$ with $xf'(x)=f'(1)$; $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\Rightarrow f=kx$.
Technique: differentiate with respect to one variable, then set the variables equal (or one of them to $0$ or $1$) to bring in the given $f'$ value. Check: $f=x^{2024}$ gives $xf'=2024f$.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of a composite of modulus and logarithm
questions.question: Consider the function $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $f(x)=e^{-|\log_e x|}$. If $m$ and $n$ be respectively the number of points at which $f$ is not continuous and $f$ is not differentiable, then $m+n$ is :
questions.key_idea: Remove the modulus: $e^{-|\ln x|}=x$ for $0<x<1$ and $\frac1x$ for $x\ge1$; only the junction $x=1$ can fail.
solution: For $0<x<1$, $|\ln x|=-\ln x$, so $f(x)=\frac1{e^{-\ln x}}=x$. For $x\ge1$, $|\ln x|=\ln x$, so $f(x)=\frac1{e^{\ln x}}=\frac1x$.
So $f(x)=x$ for $0<x<1$ and $f(x)=\frac1x$ for $x\ge1$; the graph rises along $y=x$ to the point $(1,1)$ and then falls along $y=\frac1x$.
Each piece is continuous and $\lim_{x\to1^-}x=1=f(1)=\lim_{x\to1^+}\frac1x$, so $f$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$: $m=0$.
At $x=1$ the slope on the left is $1$ and on the right is $-1$, so there is a corner: $f$ is not differentiable at exactly one point, $n=1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $e^{-|\ln x|}=\min\left(x,\frac1x\right)$: the minimum of two smooth functions has a corner only where they cross.
solution: Both $x$ and $\frac1x$ are continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, and a minimum of two continuous functions is continuous: $m=0$.
The minimum can fail to be differentiable only where the two functions are equal: $x=\frac1x\Rightarrow x=1$ (for $x>0$).
At $x=1$ their slopes are $1$ and $-1$, which differ, so there is a genuine corner: $n=1$. Hence $m+n=1$. Same answer.

useful_results: $e^{|\ln x|}=\max\left(x,\frac1x\right)$ and $e^{-|\ln x|}=\min\left(x,\frac1x\right)$ for $x>0$; in general $a^{|g|}=\max\left(a^{g},a^{-g}\right)$ for $a>1$.
The max or min of two differentiable functions is continuous, and fails to be differentiable only at crossing points where the two slopes differ.
Test any $|\,\cdot\,|$ or $\ln|\cdot|$ composite by splitting the domain at the zero of the inner expression and comparing one-sided slopes there.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of modulus functions
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\left|2x^2+5|x|-3\right|$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$. If $m$ and $n$ denote the number of points where $f$ is not continuous and not differentiable respectively, then $m+n$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Build the graph in stages: $y=2x^2+5x-3$, then $y=2x^2+5|x|-3$, then take the modulus; count the sharp corners.
solution: Start with $y=2x^2+5x-3=(2x-1)(x+3)$, a parabola with zeros at $x=-3$ and $x=\frac12$.
Replacing $x$ by $|x|$ keeps the right half and reflects it in the $y$-axis: $y=2x^2+5|x|-3$ is a 'W'-shaped curve with a corner at $x=0$ (value $-3$) and zeros at $x=\pm\frac12$.
Taking the modulus reflects the part below the $x$-axis upward: $y=\left|2x^2+5|x|-3\right|$.
$f$ is a composition of continuous functions, so it is continuous everywhere: $m=0$.
Corners of the final graph: at $x=-\frac12$ and $x=\frac12$ (where the curve meets the axis and is folded up) and at $x=0$ (the corner from $|x|$ survives as a peak of height $3$).
So $f$ is not differentiable at exactly three points $x=-\frac12,0,\frac12$: $n=3$, and $m+n=3$, option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use evenness and one-sided derivatives: $|h|$ has a corner exactly at simple zeros of $h$, and $h(|x|)$ at $0$ when $h'(0)\ne0$.
solution: $f$ is even, so work on $x\ge0$ with $h(x)=2x^2+5x-3$ and use symmetry for $x<0$.

On $x>0$ the only zero of $h$ is $x=\frac12$ (the other root is $-3$), and it is simple: $h'\left(\frac12\right)=4\cdot\frac12+5=7\ne0$. So $|h|$ has a corner at $x=\frac12$, and by symmetry at $-\frac12$.
At $x=0$: near $0^+$, $f(x)=3-5x-2x^2$ (since $h<0$), so $f'(0^+)=-5$; by evenness $f'(0^-)=+5$. The one-sided slopes differ: corner at $0$.
Elsewhere $f$ is smooth. So $n=3$, $m=0$ and $m+n=3$. Same answer.

useful_results: $|h(x)|$ is non-differentiable exactly at the zeros of $h$ where $h'\ne0$ (simple zeros); at a double zero (e.g. $|x^2|$) there is no corner.
$h(|x|)$ is an even function; it has a corner at $x=0$ iff $h'(0)\ne0$ (here $h'(0)=5$), and its other points come in pairs $\pm a$.
A composition of continuous functions is continuous, so $m=0$ whenever the formula uses only $|\cdot|$ and polynomials.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of the maximum of functions
questions.question: Let $m$ and $n$ be the number of points at which the function $f(x)=\max\{x,x^3,x^5,\dots,x^{21}\}$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, is not differentiable and not continuous, respectively. Then $m+n$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: For $|x|<1$ higher powers are closer to $0$, for $|x|>1$ they are farther; so the maximum switches only at $-1,0,1$.
solution: Compare $x^{k}$ for odd $k=1,3,\dots,21$: equal at $x=-1,0,1$; for $x<-1$ the largest is $x$ (higher odd powers are more negative), for $-1\le x<0$ the largest is $x^{21}$ (closest to $0$).
For $0\le x<1$ the largest is $x$ (higher powers are smaller), and for $x\ge1$ the largest is $x^{21}$.
At $x=-1,0,1$ the neighbouring formulas agree in value ($-1$, $0$, $1$), and each piece is continuous, so $f$ is continuous everywhere: $n=0$.
At $x=-1$ the slopes are $1$ and $21$; at $x=0$ they are $0$ (from the left, $21x^{20}\to0$) and $1$; at $x=1$ they are $1$ and $21$. All differ, so $f$ is not differentiable at $x=-1,0,1$: $m=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A finite maximum of differentiable functions can only break where two of them are equal and have different slopes: find the crossing points first.
solution: Two of the functions $x^j,x^k$ ($j\ne k$ odd) are equal when $x^j(1-x^{k-j})=0$, i.e. $x=0$ or $x^{k-j}=1$; since $k-j$ is even this gives $x=0,\pm1$. Elsewhere one function strictly leads, so $f$ is locally a single smooth power.
At each of $x=-1,0,1$ all the candidate functions take the same value ($-1,0,1$), so $f$ stays continuous: $n=0$.
At $x=\pm1$ the slopes of $x^k$ are $k$ (at $1$) or $k$ (at $-1$): $1,3,\dots,21$, all different, and the leader changes between $x$ and $x^{21}$ (slopes $1$ and $21$): a corner at each.
At $x=0$ the slopes are $1$ for $x$ and $0$ for $x^{k},k\ge3$; the leader changes between $x^{21}$ (left) and $x$ (right): a corner.

useful_results: For $\max\{x,x^3,\dots,x^{2n+1}\}$ ($n\ge1$): the function equals $x$ on $(-\infty,-1)\cup[0,1)$ and $x^{2n+1}$ on $[-1,0)\cup[1,\infty)$; it is continuous with exactly three corners $-1,0,1$.
Max or min of finitely many continuous functions is continuous; non-differentiable points are crossing points with unequal slopes.

Order of $x^k$: on $(0,1)$ larger power means smaller value; on $(1,\infty)$ larger power means larger value; for negative $x$ with odd powers the order reverses on $(-1,0)$ relative to $(-\infty,-1)$.

questions.question: The number of points of discontinuity of the function $f(x)=\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]-\left[\sqrt x\right]$, $x\in[0,4]$, where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, is ______.
questions.key_idea: Each greatest integer function jumps where its inside crosses an integer; jumps that coincide in $f$ at $x=4$ cancel.
solution: $\left[\frac{x^2}2\right]$ can jump only where $\frac{x^2}{2}$ is an integer. For $x\in[0,4]$: $0\le x^2\le16$, so $0\le\frac{x^2}2\le8$.
$x=0$ is the left end of the interval (no jump there), so $\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]$ is discontinuous at the $8$ points where $\frac{x^2}2=1,2,\dots,8$ (that is $x=\sqrt2,\dots,4$).
For $[\sqrt x]$: $0\le\sqrt x\le2$ and $\sqrt x$ is an integer for $\sqrt x=0,1,2$, i.e. $x=0,1,4$. Excluding the left end $0$, $[\sqrt x]$ is discontinuous at $x=1$ and $x=4$: $2$ points.
The point $x=4$ is common. Check it: $f(4)=8-2=6$ and $f(4^-)=7-1=6$, so $f$ is continuous at $x=4$ (the two jumps cancel).
Total points of discontinuity: $8+2-2=8$ (the point $4$ is counted twice and is not a discontinuity of $f$).
questions.correction_note: PDF writes '$\frac{x^2}{2}=0,1,\dots,8\to8$ points' (that list has nine values; $x=0$ is the left end of the interval and gives no discontinuity) and lists $x=0$ among the points for $[\sqrt x]$. Counting only the real jumps ($8$ for the first function, $x=1,4$ for the second, and the common point $x=4$ cancelling) still gives the PDF's final answer $8$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Net-jump bookkeeping: $\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]$ jumps by $+1$ and $[\sqrt x]$ by $+1$ at their critical points, and $f$ jumps by the difference.
solution: Both inner functions are continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,4]$, so each floor jumps by exactly $+1$ every time its inside reaches a new integer.
$\left[\frac{x^2}2\right]$ jumps by $+1$ at $x=\sqrt{2k}$, $k=1,\dots,8$ (eight points). $[\sqrt x]$ jumps by $+1$ at $x=1$ and $x=4$.

The jump of $f$ at a point is (jump of first) $-$ (jump of second). At $x=\sqrt{2k}\ne4$ and $x=\sqrt{2k}\ne1$ it is $+1$; at $x=1$ it is $0-1=-1$ (since $\frac{x^2}{2}=\frac12$ is not an integer there); at $x=4$ it is $1-1=0$.
Non-zero net jumps: $x=\sqrt2,2,\sqrt6,2\sqrt2,\sqrt{10},2\sqrt3,\sqrt{14}$ (seven points, $k=1,\dots,7$) and $x=1$. That is $8$ points. Same answer.

useful_results: If $g$ is continuous and strictly increasing, $[g(x)]$ jumps by exactly $1$ at every $x$ where $g(x)$ reaches an integer; the number of jumps on $[a,b]$ is the number of integers in $(g(a),g(b)]$.
In $f=[g]-[h]$ coincident jumps of the same sign cancel (continuous there), while in $[g]+[h]$ they add; always test the common points separately.
$[t+n]=[t]+n$ for an integer $n$; endpoints of the domain do not count as discontinuities from the outside, but a jump just before a right end point does.
Here: integers hit by $\frac{x^2}{2}$ in $(0,8]$: $8$; by $\sqrt x$ in $(0,2]$: $2$; common $x=4$ cancels; answer $8$.

questions.question: If the function $f(x)=\frac{\tan(\tan x)-\sin(\sin x)}{\tan x-\sin x}$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $f(0)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Continuity at $0$ means $f(0)=\lim_{x\to0}f(x)$; expand to order $x^3$ since numerator and denominator both start at $x^3$.
solution: For continuity at $0$, $f(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan(\tan x)-\sin(\sin x)}{\tan x-\sin x}$.
Expand: $\tan(\tan x)=\tan x+\frac{(\tan x)^3}{3}+\dots$ and $\sin(\sin x)=\sin x-\frac{(\sin x)^3}{3!}+\dots$ with $\tan x=x+\frac{x^3}3+\dots$, $\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\dots$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the numerator as $[\tan(\tan x)-\tan(\sin x)]+[\tan(\sin x)-\sin(\sin x)]$ and use the Mean Value Theorem and the leading term of $\tan t-\sin t$.
solution: Write $N=\tan(\tan x)-\sin(\sin x)=\left[\tan(\tan x)-\tan(\sin x)\right]+\left[\tan(\sin x)-\sin(\sin x)\right]$ and $D=\tan x-\sin x$.
First bracket: by the Mean Value Theorem, $\tan u-\tan v=\sec^2c\,(u-v)$ with $u=\tan x$, $v=\sin x$ and $c$ between them; $c\to0$, so $\sec^2c\to1$ and the bracket $\sim D$.
Second bracket: with $s=\sin x$, $\tan s-\sin s=\tan s(1-\cos s)\sim s\cdot\frac{s^2}{2}=\frac{s^3}{2}\sim\frac{x^3}2$, while $D\sim\frac{x^3}{2}$; so the second bracket $\sim D$ as well.

useful_results: $\tan x=x+\frac{x^3}3+\dots$, $\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}6+\dots$, so $\tan x-\sin x\sim\frac{x^3}{2}$; also $\tan(\tan x)\sim x+\frac{2x^3}{3}$ and $\sin(\sin x)\sim x-\frac{x^3}{3}$, giving $\tan(\tan x)-\sin(\sin x)\sim x^3$.

Hence $\frac{\tan(\tan x)-\sin(\sin x)}{\tan x-\sin x}\to2$; similarly $\frac{\tan(\tan x)-x}{x-\sin(\sin x)}\to2$ (numerator $\sim\frac{2x^3}3$, denominator $\sim\frac{x^3}{3}$). Checked symbolically.
A function defined by a $\frac00$ formula is made continuous at $a$ by defining $f(a)=\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$.
Mean Value Theorem trick: $F(u)-F(v)\approx F'(c)(u-v)$ with $c\to$ common limit; use it for differences of the same function at two nearby arguments.

concepts: Continuity and differentiability of piecewise functions with greatest integer
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}3x, & x<0\\ \min\{1+x+[x],\,x+2[x]\}, & 0\le x\le2\\ 5, & x>2\end{cases}$ where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function. If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the number of points where $f$ is not continuous and is not differentiable, respectively, then $\alpha+\beta$ equals ______.
questions.key_idea: On each unit interval $[x]$ is constant, so $f$ is a line; the candidates for trouble are only $x=0,1,2$.
solution: So $f(x)=3x$ for $x<0$; $x$ for $0\le x<1$; $x+2$ for $1\le x<2$; and $5$ for $x\ge2$. (Graph: slope-$3$ line to the origin, then $y=x$ up to the open point $(1,1)$, a jump to $(1,3)$, $y=x+2$ up to the open point $(2,4)$, then the level $5$.)
At $x=1$: $f(1^-)=1$ but $f(1)=3$, so $f$ is discontinuous. At $x=2$: $f(2^-)=4$ but $f(2)=5$, so $f$ is discontinuous. Hence $\alpha=2$ ($x\in\{1,2\}$).
Non-differentiable points: $x=1,2$ (discontinuous) and $x=0$, where the slope changes from $3$ to $1$. Hence $\beta=3$ ($x\in\{0,1,2\}$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite $f$ on $[0,2]$ as $x+\varphi([x])$ with $\varphi(n)=\min(1+n,2n)$; then only the jumps of $\varphi([x])$ at integers matter.
solution: So $f(x)=x+\varphi([x])$ on $[0,2]$ and $\varphi([x])$ changes only at integers: the jump at $x=1$ is $\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)=2\ne0$ and at $x=2$ is $\varphi(2)-\varphi(1)=1\ne0$. (The $x>2$ piece is $5=2+3$ at $x=2$, matching $f(2)=5$, but from the left $f(2^-)=4$.)
At $x=0$, $3x$ and $x$ agree in value, so $f$ is continuous; its slope changes from $3$ to $1$, so it is not differentiable there.
Hence $\alpha=2$ and $\beta=3$ (the two jump points plus the corner at $0$): $\alpha+\beta=5$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\min\{a+c,\,b+c\}=c+\min\{a,b\}$: strip the common term ($x$) first; then $\min\{1+n,2n\}$ is $0,2,3,\dots$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$ (equal at $n=1$).
A function built from $[x]$ is linear on each $[n,n+1)$; discontinuities and corners can only occur at integers (and at the junctions of given pieces such as $x=0$).
Every point of discontinuity is a point of non-differentiability, so $\alpha$-points $\subseteq$ $\beta$-points; extra $\beta$-points are the continuous corners (slope change), here $x=0$.
Check each junction in the order: left limit, value, right limit, then one-sided slopes.

questions.question: Let $[t]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$. Let $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x)=\left[\frac x2+3\right]-\left[\sqrt x\right]$. Let $S$ be the set of all points in the interval $[0,8]$ at which $f$ is not continuous. Then $\sum_{a\in S}a$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Remove the integer $3$ from the floor, locate the jumps of $\left[\frac x2\right]$ and $[\sqrt x]$, and check the common point $x=4$.
solution: $f(x)=\left[\frac x2+3\right]-\left[\sqrt x\right]=\left[\frac x2\right]-\left[\sqrt x\right]+3$, since $[t+3]=[t]+3$. For $x\in[0,8]$: $\frac x2\in[0,4]$ and $\sqrt x\in[0,2\sqrt2]$.
Points of discontinuity can occur only where $\frac x2$ is an integer or $\sqrt x$ is an integer.
$\frac x2=0,1,2,3,4$ gives $x=0,2,4,6,8$: $x=0$ is the left end (no jump there), and $2,4,6,8$ are points of discontinuity of $\left[\frac x2\right]$.
$\sqrt x=0,1,2$ gives $x=0,1,4$: $x=0$ is the left end (no jump there), and $1,4$ are points of discontinuity of $[\sqrt x]$.
So $f$ is discontinuous at $x=1,2,6,8$ for sure; $x=4$ is common and must be checked.

alternate_solutions.idea: Net-jump bookkeeping: both floors jump by $+1$ at their critical points, and $f$ jumps by the difference.
solution: $f=\left[\frac x2\right]-\left[\sqrt x\right]+3$; both inner functions are continuous and increasing, so each floor jumps by $+1$ exactly when its inside reaches a new integer.
$\left[\frac x2\right]$ jumps at $x=2,4,6,8$ (inside $=1,2,3,4$) and $[\sqrt x]$ jumps at $x=1,4$ (inside $=1,2$); $x=0$ is the left end where both are right-continuous.
Non-zero net jumps: $S=\{1,2,6,8\}$, sum $=17$. Same answer.

useful_results: $[t+n]=[t]+n$ for an integer $n$, so a constant shift of $3$ inside the bracket never changes the discontinuity set.
For $[ax]$ jumps occur at $x=\frac ka$; for $[\sqrt x]$ at perfect squares $x=k^2$; for $\left[\frac{x}{2}\right]$ at even integers. Coincident upward jumps cancel in a difference.
Always treat the interval ends carefully: at $x=8$ here the left limit is $6-2=4$ but $f(8)=7-2=5$, so $8\in S$ because $f$ is defined beyond $8$.
Here: $\{2,4,6,8\}\cup\{1,4\}$ minus the cancelled $4$ gives $\{1,2,6,8\}$.

concepts: Limits of the $1^\infty$ form and trigonometric limits
questions.question: Let $f:(0,\pi)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function given by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\left(\frac87\right)^{\frac{\tan8x}{\tan7x}}, & 0<x<\frac\pi2\\ a-8, & x=\frac\pi2\\ \left(1+|\cot x|\right)^{\frac ba|\tan x|}, & \frac\pi2<x<\pi\end{cases}$ where $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$. If $f$ is continuous at $x=\frac\pi2$, then $a^2+b^2$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Continuity gives LHL $=f\left(\frac\pi2\right)=$ RHL; the left exponent tends to $0$ and the right limit is a $1^\infty$ form giving $e^{b/a}$.
solution: $\text{LHL}=\lim_{x\to\frac\pi2^-}\left(\frac87\right)^{\frac{\tan8x}{\tan7x}}$. As $x\to\frac\pi2$: $\tan8x\to\tan4\pi=0$ while $|\tan7x|\to\infty$ ($7x\to\frac{7\pi}2$), so the exponent tends to $0$ and $\text{LHL}=\left(\frac87\right)^0=1$.
$\text{RHL}=\lim_{x\to\frac\pi2^+}\left(1+|\cot x|\right)^{\frac ba|\tan x|}$ is of the form $1^\infty$: the exponent times $|\cot x|$ is $\frac ba|\tan x||\cot x|=\frac ba$, so $\text{RHL}=e^{b/a}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Read the left exponent as $\frac0\infty$ directly, and take the logarithm of the right-hand expression to reach $\frac{\ln(1+u)}{u}\to1$.
solution: Left side: $\tan8x\to0$ (continuous at $x=\frac\pi2$ since $\tan4\pi=0$) and $|\tan7x|\to\infty$, so the exponent is of the form $\frac0\infty=0$ and $\text{LHL}=1$.
Right side: put $u=|\cot x|\to0^+$, so $|\tan x|=\frac1u$ and $\ln f(x)=\frac ba\cdot\frac{\ln(1+u)}{u}\to\frac ba$ (standard limit $\frac{\ln(1+u)}u\to1$).

Continuity: $1=a-8=e^{b/a}$, so $a=9$; $e^{b/9}=1$ forces $b=0$. (Also, $e^{r}$ is irrational for every non-zero rational $r$, so $a-8$ being an integer forces $b/a=0$ even without assuming the value $1$.)

useful_results: $\lim(1+u)^{v}=e^{\lim uv}$ when $u\to0$ and $v\to\infty$ (more generally $u\to0$ with $uv\to L$); standard forms $\frac{\ln(1+u)}{u}\to1$ and $\frac{e^u-1}{u}\to1$.
At $x=\frac\pi2$, $\tan nx$ for an integer $n$: $\to0$ if $n$ is even ($\tan\frac{n\pi}2=0$) and $|\tan nx|\to\infty$ if $n$ is odd; so $\frac{\tan8x}{\tan7x}\to0$.
$e^{r}=1\iff r=0$; $e^{r}$ is irrational for nonzero rational $r$, which is why integer-valued equalities like $e^{b/a}=a-8$ pin down the parameters.
Continuity template for a three-part definition: write LHL, value, RHL, equate; solve the parameters from the independent equalities.

concepts: Sum of squares of natural numbers
questions.question: Let for a differentiable function $f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)-f(y)\ge\log_e\left(\frac xy\right)+x-y$, $\forall x,y\in(0,\infty)$. Then $\sum_{n=1}^{20}f'\left(\frac1{n^2}\right)$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Divide by $x-y$ and let $y\to x$ from each side: the two one-sided inequalities squeeze $f'(x)=\frac1x+1$.
solution: Divide by $x-y$: for $x>y$ the inequality keeps its direction: $\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}\ge\frac{\ln x-\ln y}{x-y}+1$.
For $x<y$, $x-y<0$, so dividing reverses the inequality: $\frac{f(x)-f(y)}{x-y}\le\frac{\ln x-\ln y}{x-y}+1$. Let $y\to x^+$: $f'(x)\le\frac1x+1$ ... (2).
Since $f$ is differentiable, both one-sided limits equal $f'(x)$, so from (1) and (2): $f'(x)=\frac1x+1$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $g(x)=f(x)-\ln x-x$: the inequality says $g(x)\ge g(y)$ for all $x,y$; swapping $x,y$ forces $g$ to be constant.
solution: The inequality is $f(x)-\ln x-x\ge f(y)-\ln y-y$ for all $x,y>0$, i.e. $g(x)\ge g(y)$ with $g(t)=f(t)-\ln t-t$.
It holds for every pair, so swapping the roles gives $g(y)\ge g(x)$ as well; hence $g(x)=g(y)$ for all $x,y$: $g$ is constant.

useful_results: If $f(x)-f(y)\ge g(x)-g(y)$ for all $x,y$, then $f-g$ is constant (swap $x$ and $y$); so $f'=g'$ when both are differentiable.
Dividing an inequality by $x-y$ reverses it when $x<y$; letting $y\to x$ from both sides pins $f'(x)$ between two equal bounds. Similarly $|f(x)-f(y)|\le(x-y)^2\Rightarrow f$ is constant.
$\sum_{n=1}^{N}n^2=\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}6$; for $N=20$ it is $2870$ (checked).
Here $f(x)=\ln x+x+C$ satisfies the inequality with equality, which is a quick sanity check.

questions.question: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a twice differentiable function such that $(\sin x\cos y)\left(f(2x+2y)-f(2x-2y)\right)=(\cos x\sin y)\left(f(2x+2y)+f(2x-2y)\right)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$. If $f'(0)=\frac12$, then the value of $24f''\left(\frac{5\pi}3\right)$ is :
questions.key_idea: Collect $f(2x+2y)$ and $f(2x-2y)$: the coefficients become $\sin(x-y)$ and $\sin(x+y)$, which separates the variables.
solution: The relation is $\sin x\cos y\left[f(2x+2y)-f(2x-2y)\right]=\cos x\sin y\left[f(2x+2y)+f(2x-2y)\right]$.
Collect like terms: $f(2x+2y)\left(\sin x\cos y-\cos x\sin y\right)=f(2x-2y)\left(\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y\right)$, i.e. $f(2x+2y)\sin(x-y)=f(2x-2y)\sin(x+y)$.
Put $2x+2y=m$ and $2x-2y=n$ (independent): $\frac{f(m)}{\sin\frac m2}=\frac{f(n)}{\sin\frac n2}=K$, a constant.
questions.correction_note: PDF's last block writes '$4f''\left(\frac{5\pi}3\right)=\left(-\frac14\sin\frac{5\pi}6\right)24$': the left side should read $24f''\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)$ (a dropped digit). Also the line 'Put $x=0$; $\frac12=\frac K2$' is applied to $f'$, not $f$; it is written here as $f'(0)=\frac K2$. Answer $-3$ is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate the identity with respect to $y$ at $y=0$ to get a first-order ODE, instead of separating variables.
solution: Differentiate both sides with respect to $y$ and put $y=0$. Left: $\sin x\left[\cos y\left(2f'(2x+2y)+2f'(2x-2y)\right)-\sin y(\dots)\right]\to4\sin x\,f'(2x)$.

So $4\sin x\,f'(2x)=2\cos x\,f(2x)$. With $t=2x$: $2\sin\frac t2f'(t)=\cos\frac t2f(t)$, i.e. $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{f(t)}{\sin\frac t2}\right)=\frac{f'\sin\frac t2-\frac12f\cos\frac t2}{\sin^2\frac t2}=0$.
On $(0,2\pi)$, where $\sin\frac t2\ne0$, this gives $f(t)=K\sin\frac t2$; since $f'$ is continuous at $0$, $f'(0)=\frac K2=\frac12$ gives $K=1$ (and $\frac{5\pi}3\in(0,2\pi)$).

useful_results: $\sin x\cos y\pm\cos x\sin y=\sin(x\pm y)$: collecting $f$-terms turns this equation into $f(2x+2y)\sin(x-y)=f(2x-2y)\sin(x+y)$.
If $\frac{f(m)}{\varphi(m)}=\frac{f(n)}{\varphi(n)}$ for all independent $m,n$, then $f=K\varphi$; here $\varphi(t)=\sin\frac t2$ (with $x\pm y=\frac{m}2,\frac n2$).
For $f=K\sin\frac x2$: $f''=-\frac14f$, so $24f''\left(\frac{5\pi}3\right)=-6f\left(\frac{5\pi}3\right)=-6\sin\frac{5\pi}6=-3$ (checked symbolically, and the original identity holds identically).
Differentiating an identity in one variable and setting that variable to $0$ is a standard way to extract an ODE for $f$.

questions.question: If $y(x)=\left|\begin{matrix}\sin x&\cos x&\sin x+\cos x+1\\27&28&27\\1&1&1\end{matrix}\right|$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $C_3\to C_3-C_1$ kills two entries of the third column, so the determinant collapses to $-(1+\cos x)$.
solution: Apply $C_3\to C_3-C_1$: the third column becomes $\left(1+\cos x,\,0,\,0\right)^{T}$ (since $27-27=0$ and $1-1=0$).
Expand along the third column: $y(x)=(1+\cos x)\left(27\cdot1-28\cdot1\right)=-(1+\cos x)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The determinant is a constant-coefficient combination of $\sin x,\cos x,1$; the operator $D^2+1$ kills $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ and leaves only the constant's coefficient.
solution: Expanding along the first row, $y=A\sin x+B\cos x+C\left(\sin x+\cos x+1\right)$ where $A,B,C$ are the cofactors from rows 2 and 3, i.e. constants.
The cofactor of the entry $\sin x+\cos x+1$ is $C=\left|\begin{matrix}27&28\\1&1\end{matrix}\right|=27-28=-1$.
So $y=(A+C)\sin x+(B+C)\cos x+C$, and $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}(\sin x)=-\sin x$, $\frac{d^2}{dx^2}(\cos x)=-\cos x$, so $y''+y=C=-1$.
Hence $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+y=-1$ (no need to compute $A$ and $B$). Same answer.

useful_results: Column (row) operations $C_i\to C_i\pm C_j$ do not change a determinant; look for one that creates zeros (here $C_3-C_1$).
A determinant with one row of functions is a combination of those functions with constant cofactors as coefficients.
$(D^2+1)(a\sin x+b\cos x+c)=c$: the operator $y''+y$ removes all sine-cosine terms and returns the constant part (here $-1$); checked symbolically.
Linear differential operators with constant coefficients annihilate their own solutions; use that to skip computing derivatives.

questions.question: Let $f(x)=x^5+2x^3+3x+1$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, and $g(x)$ be a function such that $g(f(x))=x$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $\frac{g(7)}{g'(7)}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate $g(f(x))=x$, then find the $x$ with $f(x)=7$ by inspection: $f(1)=7$.
solution: $f(x)=x^5+2x^3+3x+1$, so $f'(x)=5x^4+6x^2+3>0$: $f$ is strictly increasing (so the inverse exists), and $f'(1)=5+6+3=14$.
For $f(x)=7$: $x^5+2x^3+3x+1=7$, which is satisfied by $x=1$ (and only by $x=1$, since $f$ is strictly increasing).
useful_results: If $g=f^{-1}$ then $g'(f(a))=\frac1{f'(a)}$, so $\frac{g(b)}{g'(b)}=a\,f'(a)$ where $f(a)=b$; here $a=1$ and $f'(1)=14$.
Invertibility test: $f'(x)>0$ for all $x$ (or $<0$) makes $f$ strictly monotonic, hence one-one, and the root of $f(x)=b$ is unique, so spotting one root is enough.
For a polynomial with positive coefficients, $f(1)$ is the sum of coefficients ($1+2+3+1=7$): a quick way to hit the target $7$.
Second derivative of the inverse: $g''(f(a))=-\frac{f''(a)}{\left(f'(a)\right)^3}$ (useful in the same family of questions).

questions.question: If $y(\theta)=\frac{2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta}{\cos3\theta+4\cos2\theta+5\cos\theta+2}$, then at $\theta=\frac\pi2$, $y''+y'+y$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: In terms of $c=\cos\theta$ the denominator factors as $(2c^2+2c-1)(2c+2)$, cancelling the numerator and leaving $\frac1{2(1+\cos\theta)}$.
solution: Let $c=\cos\theta$. Use $\cos2\theta=2c^2-1$ and $\cos3\theta=4c^3-3c$. The numerator is $2c+2c^2-1$.
Cancel $2c^2+2c-1$ (it equals $-1\ne0$ at $\theta=\frac\pi2$, and cancellation is valid wherever it is non-zero): $y=\frac1{2c+2}=\frac12\cdot\frac1{1+\cos\theta}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF stops at '$y''=1$' and never adds $y''+y'+y=1+\frac12+\frac12=2$; the final step was missing and has been supplied. The intermediate factorisation, $y$, $y'$ and $y''$ are all correct. Answer (A) matches the PDF key.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $y=\frac14\sec^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+u^2}4$ with $u=\tan\frac\theta2$, and differentiate through $u$ using $\frac{du}{d\theta}=\frac{1+u^2}2$.

useful_results: $\cos2\theta=2c^2-1$, $\cos3\theta=4c^3-3c$: rational functions of multiple-angle cosines become rational functions of $c=\cos\theta$, which often factor.
$1+\cos\theta=2\cos^2\frac\theta2$, hence $\frac1{1+\cos\theta}=\frac12\sec^2\frac\theta2$; in $u=\tan\frac\theta2$ one has $\frac{du}{d\theta}=\frac{1+u^2}2$.
Here $\frac{2\cos\theta+\cos2\theta}{\cos3\theta+4\cos2\theta+5\cos\theta+2}=\frac1{2(1+\cos\theta)}$ for all $\theta$ with $2c^2+2c-1\ne0$ (verified symbolically).
A cancelled factor is valid only where it is non-zero; check it at the point of evaluation.

concepts: Chain rule and product rule for composite functions
questions.question: Suppose for a differentiable function $h$, $h(0)=0$, $h(1)=1$ and $h'(0)=h'(1)=2$. If $g(x)=h\left(e^x\right)e^{h(x)}$, then $g'(0)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Product rule and chain rule; at $x=0$, $e^0=1$ so only the given values $h(0),h(1),h'(0),h'(1)$ appear.
solution: By the product and chain rules: $g'(x)=h\left(e^x\right)\cdot e^{h(x)}h'(x)+e^{h(x)}\cdot h'\left(e^x\right)e^x$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Logarithmic differentiation: $\ln g=\ln h\left(e^x\right)+h(x)$ turns the product into a sum.

useful_results: $\frac{d}{dx}h(\varphi(x))=h'(\varphi(x))\varphi'(x)$: the argument's derivative is multiplied, and $h'$ is evaluated at the inner value ($e^0=1$ here).
For a product of exponential-type factors, $\frac{g'}{g}=(\ln g)'$ avoids the product rule: $g=u\,e^{v}\Rightarrow\frac{g'}{g}=\frac{u'}{u}+v'$.
Plug $x=0$ early: only given data $h(0),h(1),h'(0),h'(1)$ survive. Checked with a cubic $h$ meeting the four conditions (it gives $4$).

questions.question: Let $f(x)=ax^3+bx^2+cx+41$ be such that $f(1)=40$, $f'(1)=2$ and $f''(1)=4$. Then $a^2+b^2+c^2$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Three conditions $f(1)$, $f'(1)$, $f''(1)$ give three linear equations; subtracting kills $a$ and shows $b+c=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $f$ as a Taylor polynomial about $x=1$ and use $f(0)=41$ to find the leading coefficient.

useful_results: A polynomial of degree $n$ is determined by its Taylor expansion at any point: $f(x)=\sum\frac{f^{(k)}(p)}{k!}(x-p)^k$; for a cubic, $f'''=6a$.
Conditions at one point ($f$, $f'$, $f''$) plus the constant term ($f(0)$) give four equations for the four coefficients of a cubic.
Pattern: $f(1)-41=a+b+c$, $f'(1)=3a+2b+c$, $f''(1)=6a+2b$; subtracting consecutive equations reduces the unknowns one at a time.

concepts: Successive differentiation (differential relation for an inverse-trigonometric exponent)
questions.question: If $\log_ey=3\sin^{-1}x$, then $\left(1-x^2\right)y''-xy'$ at $x=\frac12$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: From $\sqrt{1-x^2}\,y'=3y$, differentiate once more and multiply by $\sqrt{1-x^2}$: the expression equals $9y$.
solution: Use $\sqrt{1-x^2}\,y'=3y$: the right side is $3\cdot3y=9y$. So $\left(1-x^2\right)y''-xy'=9y$.
questions.correction_note: PDF has two typos: it writes '$(1-x)^2y''-xy'$' for $\left(1-x^2\right)y''-xy'$, and in the last lines it writes $e^{\sin^{-1}x}$ instead of $e^{3\sin^{-1}x}$ before the printed result $9e^{3\pi/6}$. The corrected working gives the same answer $9e^{\pi/2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute $x=\sin t$: the operator $\left(1-x^2\right)\frac{d^2}{dx^2}-x\frac{d}{dx}$ becomes simply $\frac{d^2}{dt^2}$.
solution: Let $x=\sin t$, so $y=e^{3t}$ and $\frac{d}{dx}=\frac1{\cos t}\frac d{dt}$.
$y_x=\frac{y_t}{\cos t}$ and $y_{xx}=\frac{y_{tt}\cos t+y_t\sin t}{\cos^3t}$, so $\left(1-x^2\right)y_{xx}=y_{tt}+y_t\tan t$ and $xy_x=y_t\tan t$.

useful_results: If $y=e^{k\sin^{-1}x}$ then $\left(1-x^2\right)y''-xy'-k^2y=0$; if $y=\sin(k\sin^{-1}x)$ or $\cos(k\sin^{-1}x)$ then $\left(1-x^2\right)y''-xy'+k^2y=0$.
With $x=\sin t$: $\left(1-x^2\right)\frac{d^2}{dx^2}-x\frac d{dx}=\frac{d^2}{dt^2}$, which explains these relations at once (checked symbolically for $k=3$).
Recognition cue: $\sqrt{1-x^2}\,y'=ky$ appears after the first differentiation of any $y=e^{k\sin^{-1}x}$; differentiate again and multiply by $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ to remove the roots.

concepts: Differentiation of product and quotient functions
questions.question: Suppose $f(x)=\frac{\left(2^x+2^{-x}\right)\tan x\sqrt{\tan^{-1}\left(x^2-x+1\right)}}{\left(7x^2+3x+1\right)^3}$. Then the value of $f'(0)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Write $f=\tan x\cdot g(x)$: since $\tan 0=0$, the product rule leaves $f'(0)=g(0)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the definition of the derivative: $f(0)=0$, so $f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)}x=\lim\frac{\tan x}{x}\,g(x)=g(0)$.
solution: $\frac{f(x)}x=\frac{\tan x}x\cdot g(x)$ with $\frac{\tan x}x\to1$ and $g$ continuous at $0$, so the limit is $g(0)$.
$g(0)=\frac{2\sqrt{\pi/4}}{1}=\sqrt\pi$. Same answer; no differentiation of the heavy expression is needed.

useful_results: If $f(x)=\varphi(x)g(x)$ with $\varphi(0)=0$, then $f'(0)=\varphi'(0)\,g(0)$; for $\varphi=\tan x$ or $\sin x$ or $x$ the factor $\varphi'(0)=1$, so $f'(0)=g(0)$.
This needs only continuity of $g$ at $0$ (via $f'(0)=\lim\frac{f(x)}{x}$), not differentiability.
Never differentiate a long product or quotient when a factor vanishes at the point: isolate that factor first (verified: $f'(0)=\sqrt\pi$ symbolically).

concepts: Successive differentiation of a logarithmic function
questions.question: Let $y=\log_e\left(\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right)$, $-1<x<1$. Then at $x=\frac12$, the value of $225\left(y'-y''\right)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the logarithm to get $y'=\frac{-4x}{1-x^4}$, then use the quotient rule once more and evaluate with $x^4=\frac1{16}$.
questions.correction_note: PDF states $y'$ and $y''$ without derivation and then jumps from the expression for $y'-y''$ to $\frac{736}{225}$ at $x=\frac12$ with no arithmetic. The derivations and the evaluation were supplied; all printed formulas are correct and the answer 736 is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split $y=\ln(1-x)+\ln(1+x)-\ln\left(1+x^2\right)$ and differentiate each logarithm: all the arithmetic at $x=\frac12$ then uses simple fractions.

useful_results: $\ln\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}$ is odd in $x$: $y'$ is even and $y''$ is odd; $y'=\frac{-4x}{1-x^4}$ in closed form.
Split $\ln\frac{u}{v}=\ln u-\ln v$ before differentiating; each $\left(\ln u\right)'=\frac{u'}u$ is simpler than the quotient rule on the whole.
$\frac d{dx}\ln\frac{1-x}{1+x}=-\frac2{1-x^2}$ and $\frac d{dx}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}=\frac2{1-x^2}$ (the inverse hyperbolic tangent pattern).

questions.question: If $f(x)=\left|\begin{matrix}2\cos^4x&2\sin^4x&3+\sin^22x\\3+2\cos^4x&2\sin^4x&\sin^22x\\2\cos^4x&3+2\sin^4x&\sin^22x\end{matrix}\right|$, then $\frac15f'(0)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the determinant one column at a time; at $x=0$ each differentiated column is zero.
solution: A determinant is differentiated column by column: $f'(x)=D_1+D_2+D_3$, where $D_i$ is $f$ with its $i$-th column differentiated and the other columns unchanged.
Column 1 has entries $2\cos^4x,\,3+2\cos^4x,\,2\cos^4x$, each with derivative $8\cos^3x(-\sin x)$.
Column 2 has entries $2\sin^4x,\,2\sin^4x,\,3+2\sin^4x$, each with derivative $8\sin^3x\cos x$.
Column 3 has entries $3+\sin^22x,\,\sin^22x,\,\sin^22x$, each with derivative $2\sin2x\cos2x\cdot2=4\sin2x\cos2x$.
At $x=0$: $\sin0=0$ and $\sin0\cos0=0$, so all three differentiated columns are zero columns.
A determinant with a zero column is $0$, so $D_1(0)=D_2(0)=D_3(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=0$.
questions.correction_note: PDF's final line shows the three determinants at $x=0$ with entries such as $\begin{vmatrix}2&0&0\\5&0&0\\2&0&0\end{vmatrix}$ that drop the unchanged columns (e.g. the third column $3,0,0$ and the second column $0,0,3$ of $f(0)$). The determinants are still $0$ because each has a zero column (the differentiated one), so the answer $0$ is unchanged; the solution is rewritten in words to avoid the wrong entries.

alternate_solutions.idea: Row operations $R_1-R_2$ and $R_3-R_2$ collapse the determinant to the constant $45$, so $f'\equiv0$.
solution: Write $a=\cos^4x$, $b=\sin^4x$, $s=\sin^22x$. Apply $R_1\to R_1-R_2$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_2$: row 1 becomes $(-3,0,3)$ and row 3 becomes $(-3,3,0)$.
Expand along the new first row: $f=-3\left(2b\cdot0-s\cdot3\right)+3\left((3+2a)\cdot3-2b\cdot(-3)\right)=9s+27+18(a+b)$.
So $f(x)=45$ for all $x$, $f'(0)=0$ and $\frac15f'(0)=0$. Same answer.

useful_results: $\frac d{dx}\det\left[C_1,C_2,C_3\right]=\det\left[C_1',C_2,C_3\right]+\det\left[C_1,C_2',C_3\right]+\det\left[C_1,C_2,C_3'\right]$ (similarly by rows).
If all the entries are even functions, the determinant is even, so $f'(0)=0$ (if $f$ is differentiable); here $\cos^4x,\sin^4x,\sin^22x$ are all even.
$\cos^4x+\sin^4x=1-\frac12\sin^22x$; with row operations this makes the determinant constant ($f\equiv45$, verified symbolically).
Before differentiating a determinant look for row or column operations that simplify it, since often it turns out to be constant.
